paper_context.research_question: Can a new formula, derived from a larger, self-built corpus, accurately assess Vietnamese text readability?
main_claims: A new, larger corpus for Vietnamese text readability assessment has been built and validated with moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa 0.422).

A new formula for Vietnamese text readability assessment has been derived using Average Sentence Length in Characters (ASLC), Average Word Length in Characters (AWLC), and Percentage of Difficult Words (PDW2) as predictors.
The new formula can predict Vietnamese text readability with an overall accuracy of 81% across different difficulty levels (Easy: 76.6%, Normal: 85.71%, Difficult: 78.45%).
Word length, sentence length, and the percentage of difficult words remain important factors in measuring Vietnamese text readability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript addresses a gap in Vietnamese text readability assessment by arguing that existing research is outdated and based on insufficient corpora. It logically proceeds to construct a new, larger, and expert-annotated corpus. This corpus then serves as the foundation for identifying key surface-level linguistic features (sentence length, word length, difficult words) highly correlated with readability. Finally, a new linear readability formula is derived using multiple regression and empirically validated through cross-validation, demonstrating its predictive accuracy across different difficulty levels. The argument flow is generally clear, moving from problem identification to solution development and empirical validation.

C1: A new, larger, and reliable corpus is essential to advance Vietnamese readability assessment (Implicit, leads to Section 3.1).
P2: A new corpus of 996 documents was built, categorized by difficulty, and annotated by Vietnamese language specialists (Claim C1).
P3: The corpus annotation demonstrates moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa 0.422), indicating its reliability (Claim C2).
C2: The newly constructed corpus provides a valid and improved foundation for deriving a modern Vietnamese readability formula (Links P2, P3).
P4: Various surface-level linguistic features (e.g., ASLS, ASLC, AWLS, AWLC, PDW1, PDW2) were extracted and their correlations with text readability were analyzed (Section 3.2, 3.3, Claim C3).
P5: ASLC, AWLC, and PDW2 were identified as highly correlated with readability and sufficiently independent for inclusion in a linear model, based on a 0.9 correlation threshold (Claim C3, C4).
C3: These selected features are appropriate and effective predictors for a linear Vietnamese readability formula (Links P4, P5).
P6: A linear readability formula was derived using multiple regression analysis with ASLC, AWLC, and PDW2 as predictors (Claim C4).
P7: The formula's performance was rigorously evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation (Section 3.3).
P8: The new formula achieved an overall predictive accuracy of 81.02% (Easy: 76.6%, Normal: 85.71%, Difficult: 78.45%) (Claim C5).
C4: The derived formula accurately predicts Vietnamese text readability across different difficulty levels (Links P6, P7, P8).
P9: Word length, sentence length, and the percentage of difficult words are confirmed as important factors in Vietnamese readability (Claim C6).
P10: Previous difficult word lists (Dien and Hao) are less effective for this corpus due to their derivation from predominantly normal readability texts (Claim C7).
C5: The new corpus and formula successfully address the limitations of prior work, offering a practical and accurate tool for Vietnamese readability assessment (Section 4).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper addresses a gap in Vietnamese text readability research by constructing a new, larger corpus and deriving a linear readability formula. The core reasoning proceeds from identifying the limitations of prior work (small, outdated corpora) to building a new corpus with expert annotations. The corpus is then analyzed for linguistic features, and correlation analysis is used to select predictors (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2). A multiple linear regression model is trained using 5-fold cross-validation to derive the formula, which is then evaluated for its predictive accuracy across three difficulty levels. The paper concludes that the formula achieves over 80% overall accuracy and that the selected features are important for Vietnamese readability. The methodology relies on the assumption that expert-labeled data, even with moderate agreement, provides a reliable ground truth, and that surface-level linguistic features can adequately model readability.
logical_argument_graph: Prior Vietnamese readability research is limited by small and outdated corpora (Section 1, 2).
Therefore, a new, larger corpus is needed to advance Vietnamese readability assessment (Section 3.1).
A new corpus of 996 documents is built and annotated by 10 experts into three difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Difficult) (Section 3.1).
Inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.422) indicates moderate reliability of the corpus annotations (Section 3.1).
Various surface-level linguistic features (sentence length, word length, percentage of difficult words/syllables) are extracted from the corpus (Section 3.2).
Correlation analysis reveals high correlations between Text Readability (TR) and ASLS, ASLC, AWLS, AWLC, and PDW2 (Table 2, Section 3.3).
To avoid multicollinearity, features with inter-correlation >= 0.9 are removed, leading to the selection of ASLC, AWLC, and PDW2 as predictors (Section 3.3).
Multiple linear regression is performed using these selected features and 5-fold cross-validation to derive a readability formula (Equation 16) (Section 3.3).

prior_stage_inputs: PAPER CONTEXT: The paper aims to assess Vietnamese text readability using a new formula derived from a self-built corpus. It identifies a gap in existing Vietnamese readability research due to small and outdated corpora. The contribution involves corpus construction, feature engineering, statistical modeling, and empirical evaluation. Main claims include building a new corpus, deriving a new formula with 81% accuracy, and confirming the importance of word/sentence length and difficult words.

SHARED ANALYSIS: Key claims extracted include the construction of a new, larger corpus with moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa 0.422), the identification of highly correlated features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2), the derivation of a new formula using these features, and its empirical accuracy (81%). Assumptions include the expertise of annotators, the validity of the scoring system, the sufficiency of Fleiss' Kappa 0.422, the linearity of readability, and the representativeness of the corpus. Uncertainty flags relate to the interpretation of kappa, the justification of feature selection thresholds, and the absence of direct comparison to prior Vietnamese formulas.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This manuscript makes a meaningful incremental contribution to the field of Vietnamese Natural Language Processing by addressing a notable gap in readability assessment. It extends existing paradigms by constructing a significantly larger and more current corpus for Vietnamese text readability, directly overcoming the limitations of previous, small, and outdated datasets. The paper then refines the application of established readability assessment techniques, specifically using surface-level linguistic features (sentence length, word length, and percentage of difficult words) and linear regression, to derive a new formula tailored for Vietnamese. This approach demonstrates semantic overlap with foundational readability research in English and earlier Vietnamese efforts, but reorganizes and updates the empirical basis for Vietnamese, providing a practical and empirically validated tool.
logical_argument_graph: Prior Vietnamese readability research is limited by small, outdated corpora (Nguyen & Henkin, 1982, 1985), necessitating an updated approach.
To address this, a new, larger corpus of 996 documents is constructed and annotated by experts across three difficulty levels, establishing a more robust ground truth for Vietnamese readability.
The corpus annotation demonstrates moderate inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa 0.422), indicating its reliability for subsequent analysis.

Drawing from established readability research, various surface-level linguistic features (e.g., sentence length, word length, difficult word percentage) are extracted and analyzed for their correlation with Vietnamese text readability.

Correlation analysis identifies Average Sentence Length in Characters (ASLC), Average Word Length in Characters (AWLC), and Percentage of Difficult Words (PDW2) as highly correlated features, which are then selected as predictors for a new formula, following a feature selection process to mitigate multicollinearity.
A new linear readability formula is derived using multiple regression analysis with the selected features, building on the established methodological paradigm of linear readability indices.
The derived formula is empirically evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrating an overall predictive accuracy of 81% across different difficulty levels.

This new corpus and formula represent a significant incremental advancement in providing a current and effective tool for Vietnamese text readability assessment, confirming the continued importance of these fundamental linguistic features.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript addresses a significant and long-standing gap in Vietnamese Natural Language Processing by developing a new, empirically-derived readability assessment formula. The core argument is that prior Vietnamese readability research is severely outdated and based on insufficient corpora, necessitating a modern approach. To this end, the authors construct a novel, larger corpus of 996 Vietnamese documents, meticulously annotated by Vietnamese language specialists into three distinct difficulty levels (Easy, Normal, Difficult). They then proceed to extract a suite of standard surface-level linguistic features, perform correlation analysis to identify key predictors, and ultimately select Average Sentence Length in Characters (ASLC), Average Word Length in Characters (AWLC), and Percentage of Difficult Words (PDW2) as the most suitable. A linear regression model is applied to these features to derive a new formula, which is subsequently evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation, demonstrating an overall prediction accuracy of 81%. The paper concludes that these fundamental linguistic features remain critical for Vietnamese readability and that the newly developed corpus and formula offer a practical and much-needed tool for various applications, from education to government documentation.
logical_argument_graph: The existing body of Vietnamese readability research is characterized by its sparsity, outdatedness, and reliance on small, unrepresentative corpora (Nguyen & Henkin, 1982, 1985).
This inadequacy creates a critical need for a modern, robust, and data-driven methodology for assessing Vietnamese text readability.
To address this, the authors undertook the construction of a new, substantially larger corpus comprising 996 Vietnamese documents, which were expertly annotated into three categories of difficulty.
The reliability of this newly constructed corpus was subsequently affirmed through an inter-annotator agreement analysis, yielding a Fleiss' Kappa score of 0.422.
A comprehensive set of surface-level linguistic features, including various measures of sentence and word length, and percentages of difficult words/syllables, were extracted from the corpus.

Correlation analysis revealed strong relationships between Average Sentence Length in Characters (ASLC), Average Word Length in Characters (AWLC), and Percentage of Difficult Words (PDW2) with overall text readability.
After a feature selection process to mitigate multicollinearity, ASLC, AWLC, and PDW2 were chosen as the optimal independent predictors for the readability formula.
Utilizing these selected features, a multiple linear regression analysis was performed to derive a novel linear formula for Vietnamese text readability.
The predictive performance of this new formula was empirically validated through 5-fold cross-validation, achieving an overall accuracy of 81%.

Therefore, the study concludes that word length, sentence length, and the percentage of difficult words are enduringly important factors in Vietnamese readability, and the derived formula, supported by the new corpus, provides an accurate and practical solution to the identified research gap.

In a sense text summarization falls also under the category of Natural Language Generation. It helps in figuring out whether or not a lengthy document meets the user’s needs and is worth reading for further information. With large texts, text summarization processes and summarizes the document in the time it would take the user to read the first paragraph. The key to summarization is to reduce the length and detail of a document while retaining its main points and overall meaning. One of the strategies most widely used by text summarization tools is sentence extraction. Important sentences from an article are statistically weighted and ranked. Summarization tools may also search for headings and other markers of subtopics in order to identify the key points of a document. The methods of summarization can be classified in two broad groups: • shallow analysis, restricted to the syntactic level of representation and try to extract significant parts of the text; • deeper analysis, assumes a semantics level of representation of the original text (typically using Information Retrieval techniques). Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

With large texts, text summarization processes and summarizes the document in the time it would take the user to read the first paragraph. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

In a sense text summarization falls also under the category of Natural Language Generation. It helps in figuring out whether or not a lengthy document meets the user’s needs and is worth reading for further information. With large texts, text summarization processes and summarizes the document in the time it would take the user to read the first paragraph. The key to summarization is to reduce the length and detail of a document while retaining its main points and overall meaning. One of the strategies most widely used by text summarization tools is sentence extraction. Important sentences from an article are statistically weighted and ranked. Summarization tools may also search for headings and other markers of subtopics in order to identify the key points of a document. The methods of summarization can be classified in two broad groups: • shallow analysis, restricted to the syntactic level of representation and try to extract significant parts of the text; • deeper analysis, assumes a semantics level of representation of the original text (typically using Information Retrieval techniques).
